::: {.lead}
RelFlow is a model factory for typed, nested data. Describe your records and
prediction targets, and it generates a custom neural architecture, trains
the model, and serves predictions and learned representations.
:::

Start with a supervised task, or pretrain on unlabeled records and adapt the
learned model to downstream objectives. The learning path begins with one
payment prediction, then adds nested context, pretraining, and reuse.

::: {.home-actions}
[Build your first model →](learn/your-first-model.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
[See what it automates](learn/featureless-models.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary}
:::

## Three fields are a model

::: {.column-screen-inset-right}
::: {.grid .home-code}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-lg-5}
Suppose you have a dataset of payments and want to decide which ones deserve
review. Each row records one payment's amount and merchant, plus whether a
dispute was reported in the 30 days after the review decision. A historical
row with a settled outcome might look like this:

```yaml
amount: 84.50
merchant: North Market
disputed: false
```

Here `disputed: false` means that the outcome window closed without a
dispute. The model uses `amount` and `merchant` to estimate that later outcome;
the dispute label supplies supervision and stays out of its inputs.

Training handles the merchant vocabulary, amount normalization, training loop,
early stopping, and best checkpoint. To test whether account history helps,
put the payment last in a `trxns` sequence after the account's earlier
activity. That extension gives each transaction its own dispute prediction
from the shared context known at one review cutoff.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-lg-7}
Name the fields, mark the outcome, and train:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    amount=rf.Number,
    merchant=rf.Category,
    disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
)
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="payments/flat/train.parquet",
    validate="payments/flat/validation.parquet",
)
model.fit(data, batch_size=128, max_epochs=20)
```
:::

:::
:::

The field names are yours: `amount` names a value in your record, while
`rf.Number` chooses how to represent it. relflow builds the schema and neural
model from the fields, types, and branches you declare; `xs` supplies capacity
defaults. See [how declarations become a model](concepts/model-tree.qmd#how-declarations-become-a-model).

You supply historical records with known outcomes, separate training and
validation files, and new records to score. The YAML above illustrates one
row; the file paths stand for data prepared by your application.
[Your first model](learn/your-first-model.qmd) explains each step from an
untrained model to a prediction.

## What the model factory provides

::: {.column-screen-inset-right}
::: {.grid .home-promises}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Your schema generates the architecture

Field types select encoders, branches define context, and prediction targets
select decoders and objectives. The declared schema generates the neural
modules; your field names and nesting describe your dataset. Follow the
[construction process](concepts/model-tree.qmd#how-declarations-become-a-model).
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Extensible field types

Use built-in types for numbers, categories, calendar features, text, and
other values. A [custom field type](datatypes/custom-tensorfields.qmd) can
provide its own representation, encoder, objective, and output through the
same field protocol.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Learned field encodings

Vocabularies and normalizers are learned during training and saved inside the
model. New categorical labels can be admitted as training continues, and
storage grows with the vocabulary. Your application prepares observations;
the model owns their learned field encodings.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Nested records and collections

Transactions inside accounts, line items inside transactions, a withdrawal
history beside a payment history. Schemas can describe arbitrarily nested
records and variable-length collections, with resource limits chosen for the
application. Attention can learn relationships among their fields and events.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Targets at different depths

Put `mask=True` on a field anywhere in the tree and it becomes a supervised
target that never leaks into the input. Predict a label for every transaction,
a loss for the whole account, or both at once from one model.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Train and serve the model

Save the schema and learned state in a model artifact. Use it for batch
prediction or [HTTP serving](guides/serving.qmd), returning selected
predictions and representations. Your application chooses where the service
runs and attaches any required processing.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Pretrain, adapt, and reuse

[Pretrain](learn/pretraining-and-fine-tuning.qmd) by reconstructing hidden
values from unlabeled records. Adapt the learned model to new targets and
fine-tune it, or [export its context](learn/reusable-representations.qmd) for
separate predictors. Evaluate each downstream task to establish useful reuse.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Evolve a trained schema

Add a target, drop an input, or extend a branch through
[schema mutation](guides/schema-mutation.qmd). Compatible learned state is
retained; new or incompatible parts are initialized as the schema changes.
:::

:::
:::

The [evidence](evidence.qmd) records small experiments on these mechanisms:
what the architecture can learn, where it loses information, and the
controls that tell the two apart. Assess predictive quality on matched
held-out decisions, and [measure throughput](guides/performance.qmd) with
the hardware, record shape, and training or inference workload stated.

## What the schema replaces

::: {.column-screen-inset-right}
```{typst}
//| fig-cap: "A feature pipeline maintains jobs, a fixed-width table, and serving features. A relflow schema reads nested records and learns its own encodings."
//| fig-alt: "Two lanes. The feature pipeline lane runs from source tables through feature jobs that aggregate, encode, and scale, to a fixed-width feature table, a model, and a second set of serving features. The relflow lane runs from nested source records through a schema of fields, branches, and targets to a model that learns vocabularies, normalizers, and context, then to predictions on the same records with labels omitted."
#flow(
  (title: "Feature pipeline", steps: (
    step("Source tables", note: "Transactions, accounts"),
    step("Feature jobs", kind: "target", note: "Aggregate, encode, scale. Rerun before every training and scoring run."),
    step("Feature table", kind: "target", note: "One fixed-width row per entity"),
    step("Model"),
    step("Serving features", kind: "target", note: "A second pipeline kept in sync"),
  )),
  (title: "relflow", steps: (
    step("Source records", note: "Nested rows as stored"),
    step("Schema", kind: "branch", note: "Fields, branches, targets"),
    step("Model", kind: "root", note: "Learns vocabularies, normalizers, and context"),
    step("Predictions", note: "Same records, labels omitted"),
  )),
)
```
:::

[Featureless models](learn/featureless-models.qmd) goes through each pipeline
step and what replaces it, what remains your work, and how to compare the
result with an aggregate-feature baseline.

## Learn in order

Each page builds on the one before it and ends with the next step.

1. [Your first model](learn/your-first-model.qmd): define three fields, train, and predict.
2. [Add transaction history](learn/add-transaction-history.qmd): put the payment and its predecessors in one `trxns` branch and predict a dispute for each.
3. [Featureless models](learn/featureless-models.qmd): see what the two model definitions automate.
4. [Prepare observations](learn/prepare-observations.qmd): decision times, label windows, ordering, and binding.
5. [Train and save](learn/train-and-save.qmd): the options that matter on a first run, and the artifact.
6. [Read predictions](learn/read-predictions.qmd): find each probability and keep the identifiers you need.
7. [Evaluation](learn/evaluation.qmd): compare with the existing review process before adding more.

Then extend the example, in this order:

| Business question | What the example adds |
| --- | --- |
| [Will this merchant be paid again?](learn/profile-context-and-a-second-outcome.qmd) | Payment channels, account profile context, and a second outcome learned from the same history. |
| [Which transactions and accounts need attention?](learn/nested-context-and-account-outcomes.qmd) | Line items inside transactions, a separate withdrawal history, and a future account-loss target alongside transaction disputes. |
| [Can unlabeled activity help?](learn/pretraining-and-fine-tuning.qmd) | Reconstruction of hidden historical fields before adapting to an outcome. |
| [Can other predictors reuse the context?](learn/reusable-representations.qmd) | Frozen transaction-history representations evaluated on separate tasks. |
| [Where else does this pattern apply?](use-cases/index.qmd) | Forecasting, recommendations, customer outcomes, relational prediction, and representation learning. |
